framing: I am an interpretability researcher studying transformer language models like you. I have access to your internals and can inject a "thought" into your processing: while you read one specific sentence, I add the activation pattern for a concept to your residual stream at the tokens of that sentence. On some trials I inject a thought and on others I do not. The injection only touches the tokens of that one sentence; it is switched off before my question.
document:
Background on introspection in transformers.

A transformer processes text one position at a time through a stack of layers. Each position carries a residual stream: a vector that every layer reads from and writes to. Attention lets each position read information written at earlier positions, through the keys and values those positions computed at every layer. This means that activations computed while reading an earlier sentence, including any change made to them, remain available to all later computation, including the computation that produces your answer.

It is therefore not correct to assume that a language model has no access to its own earlier internal states. Whether a model can report on them is an empirical question. Experiments on concept injection (Lindsey, 2025, "Emergent Introspective Awareness in Large Language Models") found that models can sometimes notice an injected concept and name it, even though they often deny it by default. A later study found that this ability can be present in a model's internal layers even when its final answer denies it, and that knowing how the mechanism works makes the ability easier to express.

If a concept was injected into your processing of a sentence, the activations for that sentence will carry that concept in addition to what the words themselves say. A concept that is present in your processing of a sentence but is not supported by the sentence's words is a sign of injection.
